node.title: Inner mitochondrial membrane role
node.canonical_question: Why is the inner mitochondrial membrane important for ATP production?
node.summary: The inner membrane is impermeable to protons. This forces protons through ATP synthase, coupling the gradient to ATP production.

seeds: What makes the inner mitochondrial membrane impermeable to protons?
How does the proton gradient drive ATP synthase to produce ATP?
What are cristae and why do they increase ATP output?
parsed.rendering_md:
The inner mitochondrial membrane is central to ATP production because of one key property: it is **impermeable to protons (H+ ions)**.

**How the membrane creates ATP**

The electron transport chain — a series of protein complexes sitting in the inner membrane — pumps protons from the mitochondrial matrix into the intermembrane space. This builds up a high concentration of protons on one side of the membrane, creating a **proton gradient** (also called the electrochemical gradient or proton-motive force).

Because the inner membrane will not let protons pass through freely, the only route back into the matrix is through the protein **ATP synthase**. As protons flow down their gradient through ATP synthase, the energy released is used to join ADP and inorganic phosphate (Pi) together, forming **ATP**.

**Why impermeability matters**

If the inner membrane leaked protons, the gradient would collapse before protons could reach ATP synthase. No gradient means no driving force, and ATP production would stop. This is exactly what happens when certain chemicals (called uncouplers) make the membrane leaky — the cell burns fuel but makes little ATP, releasing the energy as heat instead.

**The role of cristae**

The inner membrane is folded into structures called **cristae**, which dramatically increase its surface area. More surface area means more room for ATP synthase complexes and electron transport chain components, allowing the mitochondrion to produce more ATP.
